1. The discrete Fourier transform

Perhaps the most useful way to introduce the discrete Fourier transform is to look at what properties make it so important in practice. Long story short, discrete Fourier transform diagonalizes an important class of matrices, namely the discrete convolutions. Below we will see why it is so.

First, we identify the set of functions on ZN={0,1,…,N−1} {\mathbb{Z}_{N}=\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}}ZN​={0,1,…,N−1} with the vector space CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN.

On the vector space CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN, let us define a left-shift operation TL {T_{L}}TL​ on CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN, which maps any vector in CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN

a=(a0a1⋯aN−1)T↦TL(a):=(a1a2⋯a0)T.\displaystyle {\bf a}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{0} & a_{1} & \cdots & a_{N-1}\end{pmatrix}^{T}\mapsto T_{L}({\bf a}):=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1} & a_{2} & \cdots & a_{0}\end{pmatrix}^{T}.a=(a0​​a1​​⋯​aN−1​​)T↦TL​(a):=(a1​​a2​​⋯​a0​​)T.

It is easy to check that this left-shift operation TL {T_{L}}TL​ is a linear transformation on CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN, which can be written as a matrix

TL=(11⋱11)\displaystyle T_{L}=\begin{pmatrix} & 1\\ & & 1\\ & & & \ddots\\ & & & & 1\\ 1 \end{pmatrix}TL​=​1​1​1​⋱​1​​

multiplying on the left of the vector a {{\bf a}}a. The right-shift operation is defined as TR:=TL−1 {T_{R}:=T_{L}^{-1}}TR​:=TL−1​. We are interested in the eigenvectors of this matrix TL {T_{L}}TL​.

Exercise 1 Check that a set of eigenvectors {ek}k=0N−1⊂CN {\{{\bf e}^{k}\}_{k=0}^{N-1}\subset\mathbb{C}^{N}}{ek}k=0N−1​⊂CN of the matrix TL {T_{L}}TL​ are

ek=(1e2πik/Ne2⋅2πik/N⋯e(N−1)2πik/N)T.\displaystyle {\bf e}^{k}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & e^{2\pi ik/N} & e^{2\cdot2\pi ik/N} & \cdots & e^{(N-1)2\pi ik/N}\end{pmatrix}^{T}.ek=(1​e2πik/N​e2⋅2πik/N​⋯​e(N−1)2πik/N​)T.

Writing it more systematically, we denote the N×N {N\times N}N×N matrix

F=(e0e1⋯eN−1)\displaystyle F=\begin{pmatrix}{\bf e}{}^{0} & {\bf e}{}^{1} & \cdots & {\bf e}^{N-1}\end{pmatrix}F=(e0​e1​⋯​eN−1​)

and we see that

TLF=FΛ:=F(10e2πik/N⋱0e(N−1)2πik/N).\displaystyle T_{L}F=F\Lambda:=F\begin{pmatrix}1 & & & 0\\ & e^{2\pi ik/N}\\ & & \ddots\\ 0 & & & e^{(N-1)2\pi ik/N} \end{pmatrix}.TL​F=FΛ:=F​10​e2πik/N​⋱​0e(N−1)2πik/N​​.

Exercise 2 Show that F−1=1NF∗ {F^{-1}=\frac{1}{N}F^{*}}F−1=N1​F∗, where F∗ {F^{*}}F∗ is the Hermittian transpose of F {F}F. Therefore, the above can be written as

1NF∗TLF=Λ.\displaystyle \frac{1}{N}F^{*}T_{L}F=\Lambda.N1​F∗TL​F=Λ.

Now we employ a crucial result from linear algebra.

Exercise 3 Let A,B {A,B}A,B be matrices with entries in C {\mathbb{C}}C. Suppose that two matrices commute, that is

AB=BA.\displaystyle AB=BA.AB=BA.

And suppose further that the matrix B {B}B has N {N}N distinct eigenvalues. Then every eigenvector of B {B}B is also an eigenvector of A {A}A. Consequently, A {A}A can diagonalized by the same matrices that diagonalize B {B}B.

This result leads us to consider what matrices commute with TL {T_{L}}TL​. It is quite easy to find these matrices: they are circulant matrices, which are of the form

Ta:=(a0aN−1⋯a1a1a0⋯a2⋮⋱aN−1aN−2⋯a0),a=(a0a1⋮aN−1)∈CN.\displaystyle T_{{\bf a}}:=\begin{pmatrix}a_{0} & a_{N-1} & \cdots & a_{1}\\ a_{1} & a_{0} & \cdots & a_{2}\\ \vdots & & & \ddots\\ a_{N-1} & a_{N-2} & \cdots & a_{0} \end{pmatrix},\quad{\bf a}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{0}\\ a_{1}\\ \vdots\\ a_{N-1} \end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}.Ta​:=​a0​a1​⋮aN−1​​aN−1​a0​aN−2​​⋯⋯⋯​a1​a2​⋱a0​​​,a=​a0​a1​⋮aN−1​​​∈CN.

The linear transformations on CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN associated to these circulant matrices are called discrete convolutions.

Exercise 4 Let a,b∈CN {{\bf a},{\bf b}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}}a,b∈CN. The discrete convolution of a {{\bf a}}a and b {{\bf b}}b is denoted as a∗b:=Tab {{\bf a}*{\bf b}:=T_{{\bf a}}{\bf b}}a∗b:=Ta​b. Show that

(a∗b)i=(Tab)i=∑k=0N−1ai−kbk,i=0,…,N−1\displaystyle ({\bf a}*{\bf b})_{i}=(T_{{\bf a}}{\bf b})_{i}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_{i-k}b_{k},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1(a∗b)i​=(Ta​b)i​=k=0∑N−1​ai−k​bk​,i=0,…,N−1

where indices are modulo N {N}N as appropriate.

As a consequence of Exercise 3, we see that circulant matrices Ta {T_{{\bf a}}}Ta​ are diagonalized by the matrix F {F}F

1NF∗TaF=ΛTa.\displaystyle \frac{1}{N}F^{*}T_{{\bf a}}F=\Lambda_{T_{{\bf a}}}.N1​F∗Ta​F=ΛTa​​.

And we will refer the linear transformation F−1 {F^{-1}}F−1 as the discrete Fourier transform.
Now let's look at some examples.

Example 1 The central difference scheme of the second derivative with periodic boundary condition uses the following matrix

(−2111−211−21⋱11−2)\displaystyle \begin{pmatrix}-2 & 1 & & & 1\\ 1 & -2 & 1\\ & 1 & -2 & 1\\ & & & \ddots\\ 1 & & & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}​−211​1−21​1−2​1⋱1​1−2​​

can be diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform.

1n∑i=1npi(0)=0.\displaystyle \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{(0)}=0.n1​i=1∑n​pi(0)​=0.

pi(k)=12(pi(k−1)+pi+1(k−1))\displaystyle p_{i}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{i}^{(k-1)}+p_{i+1}^{(k-1)}\right)pi(k)​=21​(pi(k−1)​+pi+1(k−1)​)

and we consider p1(k) {p_{1}^{(k)}}p1(k)​ and pn(k) {p_{n}^{(k)}}pn(k)​ to be also neighboring points. Show that these n {n}n points converge to the origin.

Exercise 6 What is the matrix for the central difference scheme with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition? Can you still diagonalize it with discrete Fourier transform?

Exercise 7 What is the matrix for the central difference scheme with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition? Can you still diagonalize it with discrete Fourier transform?

Example 2 The previous JPEG standards uses discrete cosine transform (DCT). It can be regarded as a special case of the discrete Fourier transform. In one-dimension, it amounts to extend the image on ZN {\mathbb{Z}_{N}}ZN​ evenly on Z2N {\mathbb{Z}_{2N}}Z2N​. Of course these is also a discrete sine transform. The current JPEG-2000 standard uses wavelet transforms, which is beyond the scope here.

Exercise 8 The auto-correlation of a vector v∈CN {{\bf v}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}}v∈CN is defined to be

r=Tv‾v\displaystyle {\bf r}=T_{\overline{{\bf v}}}{\bf v}r=Tv​v

where Tv‾ {T_{\overline{{\bf v}}}}Tv​ is defined as before, vˉ {\bar{{\bf v}}}vˉ is the entry-wise complex conjugation of v {{\bf v}}v. What are the discrete Fourier coefficients of r {{\bf r}}r?

2. The fast Fourier transform: FFT

Let us denote the discrete Fourier transform matrix on CN {\mathbb{C}^{N}}CN to be FN {F_{N}}FN​. For example,

F2=(111−1)\displaystyle F_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}F2​=(11​1−1​)

and

F4=(11111i−1−i1−11−11−i−1i).\displaystyle F_{4}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & i & -1 & -i\\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1\\ 1 & -i & -1 & i \end{pmatrix}.F4​=​1111​1i−1−i​1−11−1​1−i−1i​​.

The whole thing of FFT is the observation that FN {F_{N}}FN​ and FN/2 {F_{N/2}}FN/2​ is related. So that when N=2n {N=2^{n}}N=2n, an extremely efficent algorithm can be designed, implicitly computing the matrix multiplication y=FNx {{\bf y}=F_{N}{\bf x}}y=FN​x.
What is the relation between FN {F_{N}}FN​ and FN/2 {F_{N/2}}FN/2​? Recall that

(FN)j,k=e2πijk/N.\displaystyle (F_{N})_{j,k}=e^{2\pi ijk/N}.(FN​)j,k​=e2πijk/N.

So

(FN/2)m,l=(FN)2m,l=(FN)m,2l.\displaystyle (F_{N/2})_{m,l}=(F_{N})_{2m,l}=(F_{N})_{m,2l}.(FN/2​)m,l​=(FN​)2m,l​=(FN​)m,2l​.

There are remaining entries in FN {F_{N}}FN​ that are not in FN/2 {F_{N/2}}FN/2​. But these entries are those with double odd indices, each of which differs from its nearby even-index entries in the same row by a power of e2πi/N {e^{2\pi i/N}}e2πi/N, depending which row it lies. We are thus inspired to separate the input according to its indice's parity.
Take N=4 {N=4}N=4 for an example. Let x=(x0x1x2x3)T {{\bf x}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{0} & x_{1} & x_{2} & x_{3}\end{pmatrix}^{T}}x=(x0​​x1​​x2​​x3​​)T. We write

x′=(x0x2)Tx′′=(x1x3)T.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} {\bf x}' & = & \begin{pmatrix}x_{0} & x_{2}\end{pmatrix}^{T}\\ {\bf x}'' & = & \begin{pmatrix}x_{1} & x_{3}\end{pmatrix}^{T}. \end{array}x′x′′​==​(x0​​x2​​)T(x1​​x3​​)T.​

And suppose F2 {F_{2}}F2​ is known. So here we can compute

y′=F2x′y′′=F2x′′\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} {\bf y}' & = & F_{2}{\bf x}'\\ {\bf y}'' & = & F_{2}{\bf x}'' \end{array}y′y′′​==​F2​x′F2​x′′​

How do we get F4x {F_{4}{\bf x}}F4​x from y′ {{\bf y'}}y′ and y′′ {{\bf y}''}y′′? Inspecting closely the matrix F4 {F_{4}}F4​, we see that

F4x=(1111 )(111−1 )(x0x2 )+(1i−1−i)( 111−1)( x1x3)=(111i1−11−i)(111−1 )(x0x2 )+(111i1−11−i)( 111−1)( x1x3)=(111i1−11−i)(111−1111−1)(1111)(x0x1x2x3)\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} & F_{4}{\bf x}\\ & = & \begin{pmatrix}1\\ & 1\\ 1\\ & 1 & & \, \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\\ \\ & & & \, \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_{0}\\ x_{2}\\ \\ \, \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix} & & 1\\ & & & i\\ & & -1\\ & & & -i \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\,\\ \\ & & 1 & 1\\ & & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\,\\ \\ x_{1}\\ x_{3} \end{pmatrix}\\ & = & \begin{pmatrix}1 & & 1\\ & 1 & & i\\ 1 & & -1\\ & 1 & & -i \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\\ \\ & & & \, \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_{0}\\ x_{2}\\ \\ \, \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1 & & 1\\ & 1 & & i\\ 1 & & -1\\ & 1 & & -i \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\,\\ \\ & & 1 & 1\\ & & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\,\\ \\ x_{1}\\ x_{3} \end{pmatrix}\\ & = & \begin{pmatrix}1 & & 1\\ & 1 & & i\\ 1 & & -1\\ & 1 & & -i \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\\ & & 1 & 1\\ & & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ & & 1\\ & 1\\ & & & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_{0}\\ x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ x_{3} \end{pmatrix} \end{array}​F4​x===​​11​11​​​​​11​1−1​​​​​x0​x2​​​+​​​1−1​i−i​​​​​11​1−1​​​x1​x3​​​​11​11​1−1​i−i​​​11​1−1​​​​​x0​x2​​​+​11​11​1−1​i−i​​​​​11​1−1​​​x1​x3​​​​11​11​1−1​i−i​​​11​1−1​11​1−1​​​1​1​1​1​​​x0​x1​x2​x3​​​​

And factorising the F4 {F_{4}}F4​ into three matrices is essentially what FFT is doing. Notice that in the factorization of F4 {F_{4}}F4​, each matrix has a lot more zeros (each row has no more that two nonzero terms). This is essentially why FFT is fast.
In general, the idea is the same. We have

yj=yj′+ej⋅2πi/Nyj′′,j=0,…,N/2−1\displaystyle y_{j}=y_{j}'+e^{j\cdot2\pi i/N}y''_{j},\quad j=0,\dots,N/2-1yj​=yj′​+ej⋅2πi/Nyj′′​,j=0,…,N/2−1

yj+N/2=yj′−ej⋅2πi/Nyj′′,j=0,…,N/2−1\displaystyle y_{j+N/2}=y_{j}'-e^{j\cdot2\pi i/N}y''_{j},\quad j=0,\dots,N/2-1yj+N/2​=yj′​−ej⋅2πi/Nyj′′​,j=0,…,N/2−1

What is the computational cost of FFT? We can preorder the input using the binaries. So the permutations can be ignored. Then to go from the one level to the next, we need only perform O(N) {O(N)}O(N) additions and multiplications, there are n=log⁡2N {n=\log_{2}N}n=log2​N levels, so the total computational cost is O(Nlog⁡N) {O(N\log N)}O(NlogN).
